cards.hook: An index is less volatile than the stocks inside it.
cards.body: Index variance isn't the average of its members' variances. It's that average scaled down by how loosely the names move together. When correlation sits below one, the diversification nets out idiosyncratic moves, so **index implied vol trades below the average vol of its components**. That gap is itself a tradeable quantity: implied correlation. Dispersion desks sell the richer index volatility and buy the cheaper single-name volatility, harvesting the spread. The position is really a short bet on correlation. It pays in calm, stock-picking regimes and gets run over when everything crashes together and correlation snaps toward one.
cards.depth: The crash risk is the whole story. In a selloff correlations converge toward one, the diversification benefit vanishes, and the short-correlation book loses on both legs at once. That is why implied correlation sits above realized, much the way index vol sits above realized vol. You are paid to hold a tail, not to be clever.

cards.hook: A test's accuracy tells you almost nothing on its own.
cards.body: Bayes runs on odds, not percentages, and that reframing kills most intuition errors. Posterior odds equal prior odds times a single number, the **likelihood ratio**: how much more often you'd see this evidence if the claim were true than if it were false. A '95% accurate' test with a matching false-positive rate carries a likelihood ratio around 19. Against a 1-in-1,000 prior, that leaves you under 2% even after a positive result. The accuracy figure is a distraction; the ratio and the base rate are the whole calculation. Weighing any evidence, a deposition, a signal, a screen, asks the same two questions.
cards.depth: The trap is updating on how strong the evidence sounds while ignoring how rare the thing was to begin with. A damning-sounding fact with a likelihood ratio of 3 moves a one-in-a-thousand prior to roughly one in 333. Still almost certainly innocent. Strong-sounding is not the same as diagnostic.

cards.hook: You can't feel time passing. So what do you do instead?
cards.body: Willpower won't fix a measurement deficit, so don't aim there. The move from before: stop querying the clock and **make time occupy space you can see**. A depleting visual timer, the shrinking colored disc of a Time Timer, converts an invisible quantity into a shape that visibly contracts in your field of view. The whole point is passive glanceability, because the act of stopping to check the time is exactly the act that never happens. You read what's left at a glance, with no self-initiated query required.
cards.depth: This is the same logic as anchoring a pill to your coffee: don't ask the weak executive function to do the work, offload the job to the environment. Any invisible variable you keep losing to, time, money burn, open task count, gets more reliable the moment you give it a physical, glanceable form.

cards.hook: One actress's lawsuit capped every Hollywood contract at seven years.
cards.body: Studios in the 1930s held actors to seven-year contracts, then stretched them. Refuse a role, you got suspended, and the suspension time was tacked onto the end, so a seven-year deal could run indefinitely. In 1944 Olivia de Havilland sued Warner Bros. and won: California's limit on personal-service contracts means **seven calendar years, not seven years of actual work**. Section 2855 of the Labor Code still carries that cap. Decades later recording artists have invoked the same statute against labels that tried to measure a contract in albums delivered rather than years elapsed.
cards.depth: The rhyme is control dressed as a term of art. Then it was suspension clauses; now it's options, exclusivity windows, and delivery-based terms that count a deal in output, not time. The de Havilland principle keeps resurfacing because the incentive to lock talent up never left, only the drafting did.

cards.hook: Checking an answer is easier than producing one. Build on that.
cards.body: The most useful asymmetry in LLM system design is the gap between generating and verifying. A model that struggles to produce a correct answer can often reliably judge whether a candidate answer is correct, because judging needs less of the open-ended search that generation does. **Architect the generator and the verifier as separate roles.** Sample several candidates cheaply, then spend your reliability budget on a verifier that kills the bad ones. It's why best-of-N sampling, LLM-as-judge, and adversarial checking work at all. One confident pass is the weakest design; a mediocre generator plus a strict verifier beats it.
cards.depth: The failure mode is letting the same model, same prompt, grade itself, which just re-confirms its first mistake. The verifier has to differ: a new lens, a demand to locate the evidence rather than opine on it, or an adversary told to refute. Diversity in the checker is what makes the asymmetry pay.

cards.hook: The VIX isn't a price. You can't actually trade it.
cards.body: The VIX is a calculation squeezed out of a strip of SPX option prices, engineered to express 30-day implied variance as a single constant-maturity number. Nothing holds that number. What trades is VIX futures, each with its own expiry and its own level, usually in contango above spot. So when spot VIX spikes 40%, your front-month future might move 15%, and your VIX-linked ETP decays as it rolls up the curve. **You are long the futures curve, not the index.** Treating the quoted VIX as your exposure is the first mistake.
cards.depth: Spot and the futures converge only at expiration. Between now and then, roll yield dominates. In calm regimes contango bleeds a long-vol position daily even if realized vol never falls. That bleed is the exact mirror of the premium short-vol sellers collect for sitting on the other side.

cards.hook: Your lisdexamfetamine does nothing until your blood cuts it apart.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug: dextroamphetamine chemically bonded to the amino acid lysine, which is inert. It only becomes active after enzymes in your red blood cells cleave the lysine off, and that conversion runs at a roughly fixed rate no matter how fast you swallow it. **The bloodstream, not the pill coating, is the time-release mechanism.** That is why it ramps smoothly, why crushing or chewing it changes little, and why an empty stomach barely speeds onset.
cards.depth: The practical move: onset is set by your metabolism, not by timing tricks, so take it at the same clock time daily and judge the curve across a week, not one morning. Heavy acid loads near the dose (citrus, high-dose vitamin C) can blunt amphetamine absorption, so space them out.

cards.hook: You can be perfectly calibrated and still completely useless.
cards.body: Calibration means your 70% forecasts come true 70% of the time. You can guarantee it trivially: predict the base rate for everything. If it rains 30% of days, say "30%" every single day and you will be flawlessly calibrated and worthless, because you never told anyone which days. The missing ingredient is **resolution: how far you dare to move off the base rate and still land right.** Elite forecasters are both calibrated and high-resolution. Scoring only one of the two hides the sharpest signal of actual skill.
cards.depth: The Brier score decomposes exactly into calibration, resolution, and irreducible uncertainty. A superforecaster's edge lives in resolution: pushing confident calls toward 95% or 5% and being correct there. Rewarding calibration alone rewards timidity, and quietly promotes the forecaster who hedges everything.

cards.hook: California now protects the dead from digital replicas too.
cards.body: Everyone tracked AB 2602, the 2024 law letting living performers void vague AI digital-replica clauses. Its quieter sibling, AB 1836, aimed at the dead. It requires consent from a deceased personality's estate before using an AI-generated replica of their voice or likeness in most expressive works, backed by statutory damages. **The post-mortem right of publicity now has explicit teeth against synthetic resurrection.** For documentary, biopic, and archival work, "they're gone, so clear it with no one" is no longer a safe assumption in California.
cards.depth: Both took effect in 2025. Carve-outs exist for news, public affairs, satire, and certain documentary uses, but they are narrower than practitioners assume and do not cover a fabricated performance stitched together to sell something. Estate sign-off, not a general fair-use shrug, is the clearance path.

cards.hook: Recall it: you tuned six parameters on three years. The cost?
cards.body: The answer is degrees of freedom. Every parameter you optimize against the same fixed history is a knob you turned until the past looked good. With six knobs and one dataset you are no longer testing a hypothesis, you are drawing a curve through your own noise. **More free parameters demand exponentially more independent data before the result means anything.** The tell is a backtest that dazzles in-sample and dies the month you trade it, because the only thing it learned was last cycle's accidents.
cards.depth: A rough discipline: count your free parameters, then ask whether your sample holds enough genuinely independent regimes to support them. Walk-forward testing and a deflated Sharpe ratio exist to charge you for the search. If you can't say how many variations you tried, you can't trust the one you kept.

cards.hook: Long volatility bleeds even when the market does nothing.
cards.body: VIX futures usually trade in contango: contracts further out price higher than spot, because fear is expected to mean-revert upward from calm. If you hold a long-vol position built from those futures, each day they roll down the curve toward a lower spot, and you lose that difference even when realized volatility never moves. **Contango is rent you pay to stay long fear.** This is why long-vol ETPs grind lower for years, then spike. The structure quietly taxes patience and rewards only precise timing.
cards.depth: Flip it: in backwardation, when spot vol sits above the futures, the roll pays you to stay long. That regime shows up in a crisis and vanishes fast, which is exactly when holding vol is both cheapest to carry and most valuable.

cards.hook: SAG-AFTRA split digital replicas in two. Consent differs.
cards.body: The 2023 TV/theatrical contract drew a line practitioners still blur. An **employment-based digital replica** is made from a performer's work on that specific job; an independently created one is built outside it. Both need the performer's clear, separately bargained consent, and the consent must describe the actual uses, not grant a blanket license. A signature on the deal memo does not cover a replica. The frontier fight now is how specific 'specific use' has to be, and whether that consent can survive to the next production.
cards.depth: The trap is treating replica consent like a standard likeness clause. It is closer to a per-use license: scope it to the project, the medium, and the term, because a vague grant is exactly what newer state statutes are starting to void.

cards.hook: You give a 90% sure range. How often is it right?
cards.body: Take a beat before the number lands. Most people, asked for a range they are 90 percent confident contains the truth, are right far less than that. Reported calibration studies cluster the real hit rate around **40 to 50 percent**, not 90. The cause is anchoring: you fix on a best guess, then widen the edges too timidly, so your 'wide' interval still hugs your point estimate. The fix stays mechanical. Set the range, then stretch it until it feels absurd, because absurd is usually where calibrated lives.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: every position size, every deal reserve, every 'worst case' you set runs on an interval. If the interval is secretly a coin flip, so is the cushion you built on it. Widen first, then size.

cards.hook: Open loops run in your head rent-free. Close them on paper.
cards.body: An unfinished intention tends to stay active in memory, nagging for attention until it is either done or recorded somewhere you trust. That background hum is cheap for most brains and expensive for yours, because **working memory is your scarcest resource** and every live 'I need to...' is holding a slot. The move is not to try harder to remember. It is to dump each open loop into one capture spot the instant it appears, so the loop closes externally and stops firing while you work the task in front of you.
cards.depth: The capture spot only works if it is single and trusted. Two lists, or one you doubt, and the brain keeps holding the loop as backup, which defeats the offload. One inbox, reviewed on a schedule, is what lets you actually let go.

cards.hook: Your backtest fills at a price the market never offered.
cards.body: Most backtests assume you buy and sell at the closing or midpoint price. Real orders cross the bid-ask spread, suffer slippage when size moves the book, and pay impact in thin names. None of that appears in the equity curve, so a strategy looks clean on screen and bleeds in production. **The more it trades, the bigger the fantasy.** A high-turnover edge that earns a few basis points per trade gross can go flatly negative once realistic costs land on every fill.
cards.depth: Test it honestly: re-run assuming fills at the far side of the spread plus a slippage estimate, and scale costs with your order size versus average volume. If the edge dies under that, it was never an edge, just an accounting artifact.

cards.hook: Full Kelly maximizes growth. Half-Kelly keeps most of it.
cards.body: Bet the full Kelly fraction and you maximize long-run geometric growth. The catch: the growth curve is flat on top. Because growth falls off quadratically around the optimum, betting **half of Kelly surrenders only about a quarter of your growth rate while cutting volatility roughly in half.** Overbet instead and the penalty is not symmetric: at twice Kelly your expected growth drops to zero. Since you never know your true edge, and overestimating it pushes you past the peak, sizing below the estimate is cheap insurance. Most pros who invoke Kelly actually run a fraction of it.
cards.depth: The asymmetry is the whole point. A measurement error that makes you overbet costs far more growth than the same error underbetting, because the right half of the curve falls to zero while the left half stays gentle. When your edge is uncertain, shrink the fraction. The uncertainty itself is a reason to bet smaller, not a detail to ignore.

cards.hook: Punishment seems to work, praise seems to fail. Neither is true.
cards.body: Performance has a skill component and a luck component. Extreme results lean on luck, and luck does not repeat, so the next attempt drifts back toward the average no matter what you did in between. **The intervention gets credit that belongs to regression to the mean.** Scream at a pilot after a terrible landing and the next one improves; praise one after a brilliant landing and the next is worse. The feedback felt causal. It was arithmetic. Any time you act only on an extreme reading, expect the follow-up to look like your action worked, or backfired, when it did neither.
cards.depth: The rule of thumb: whenever a correlation is imperfect, there will be regression, and the weaker the true signal the more any outlier is just noise that reverses. It is why the rookie of the year slumps, why the fund on the magazine cover lags next year, and why you judge an intervention against a control group, never against the before-reading that triggered it.

cards.hook: A silent witness lowers the cost of starting.
cards.body: Activation, not motivation, is the bottleneck: the task sits because the brain cannot generate enough arousal to cross the starting threshold. A second person present, even one doing unrelated work and saying nothing, supplies that arousal from outside. Mild social presence raises alertness and adds light accountability, and together they push you over a line you could not cross alone. **This is body doubling, and the mechanism is external activation, not willpower borrowed from someone else.** The move: schedule a standing silent co-working call for the task you keep deferring. The partner's only job is to exist on the screen.
cards.depth: Why it beats a reminder: a reminder re-states the task you already know. Body doubling changes your physiological state instead. It works best on activation-gated chores, admin, email, filing, and worst on tasks needing deep private thought, where another presence becomes noise. Match the tool to the failure. Use it when starting is the problem, not when sustained focus is.

cards.hook: Your AI consent was for one job, not all of them.
cards.body: The 2023 SAG-AFTRA film and television contract did not ban digital replicas. It made **consent specific and non-transferable the default.** A studio that scans a performer to build a digital replica needs a clear, separate consent describing how the replica will be used, and use outside that description requires fresh consent and additional pay. Consent on one production does not travel to the next, and in most cases use after death still requires consent from the performer's estate. The practitioner error is treating an AI-replica clause like a standard work-for-hire grant. It behaves more like a license with a scope you must police.
cards.depth: The deeper shift is drafting posture. A digital-replica right now reads like a scoped license: who, which production, what uses, what duration, renewable only by new consent. Broad or vague grants are exactly what the newer California and New York replica statutes also target. Paper it as a blanket assignment and you are both out of step with the guild floor and likely unenforceable under state law.

cards.hook: The short-vol trade that had to buy exactly what was killing it.
cards.body: On February 5, 2018, the VIX nearly doubled in a day. That alone was survivable. The structural killer was mechanical: inverse-volatility products like the XIV note had to rebalance daily, and a spike forced them to **buy VIX futures into the close, in a size larger than the market could absorb.** Their own required buying pushed futures higher, which forced still more buying, a reflexive loop. XIV fell roughly 96% and was terminated within days. The lesson is not 'volatility is dangerous.' It is that a product with forced, size-insensitive rebalancing becomes its own worst counterparty in a crisis.
cards.depth: The tell was visible beforehand. Assets in short-vol products had ballooned, so the end-of-day rebalance buy was always going to be huge relative to VIX futures liquidity. Anyone sizing that hedge against daily volume saw the trap. The same feature shows up in any strategy that must trade a fixed rule regardless of price, with portfolio insurance in 1987 as the ancestor.

cards.hook: A calendar spread wants stillness now and higher vol later.
cards.body: Sell the near-dated option, buy the far-dated one at the same strike, and you hold a position with split personalities. The near leg carries more gamma and decays faster, so net you are short gamma and long theta: you profit when the stock sits still and bleed if it jumps. The far leg carries more vega, so you are also long volatility. **The spread pays you to be right about calm now and nervous later.** It is the rare structure that is at once a bet on realized quiet and on implied vol rising into the back month.
cards.depth: Watch the trap: the position is long vega but short gamma, so a sharp move can lose even as the vol you wanted finally shows up. The move hurts through gamma before the vol rise helps through vega. Size it as a view on the term structure of volatility, not on direction.

cards.hook: The Copyright Office split your AI comic in two.
cards.body: In 2023 the US Copyright Office ruled on Zarya of the Dawn, a comic whose images came from Midjourney. It did not reject the work wholesale. It canceled the original registration and reissued a narrower one: the human-written text and the selection, coordination, and arrangement of the images were protected, but **the individual AI-generated images were not authored by a human**, so they got nothing. Practitioners keep saying AI work is flatly uncopyrightable. The real rule is more surgical: the human's creative choices around the output can be protected while the output itself stays unprotected.
cards.depth: The line is human authorship, applied element by element, not work by work. A prompt is treated more like a commission than like drawing. So the protectable layer is whatever a person actually selected, edited, or arranged. Register those choices explicitly and disclaim the generated pixels.

cards.hook: When a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring.
cards.body: This is Goodhart's law, and it is the quiet killer in both your worlds. A number works as a signal only while nobody is optimizing it directly. The moment it becomes the goal, people and systems route around its intent while hitting its letter. **Optimizing the metric and achieving the thing it stood for are not the same act.** A backtest tuned to maximize Sharpe stops predicting live Sharpe. Billable-hour targets grow hours, not value. Teaching to the test raises scores, not learning. The cure is to keep the true objective and the measured proxy visibly separate.
cards.depth: The sharper version is Campbell's law: the more a quantitative measure drives decisions, the more it corrupts the process it was meant to monitor. The defense is to hold several proxies that are hard to game at once, and to re-check whether the proxy still tracks the thing you actually want.

cards.hook: Starting is half of it. You also can't stop.
cards.body: The executive-function cost that blocks starting a task also blocks ending one. Disengaging requires shifting set, pulling attention off a loaded context, and that switch is exactly the weak link. So hyperfocus is not a power you summoned; it is a brake that failed. The concrete move is to **build the exit ramp before you enter**: set a hard external stop tied to a real obligation, not a vague intention. An alarm across the room you must stand up to silence, a meeting at the hour, a person expecting you. Pre-commit the stop while you still have the judgment to.
cards.depth: Why the external cue: once you are in, the same system that cannot switch also cannot notice it should. An internal reminder loses to the task every time. A stop that forces a physical action or involves another human borrows the salience your attention cannot generate from inside the tunnel.

cards.hook: Recall it: your screen reads last quarter's EPS. The trap?
cards.body: Give it a beat before the answer. The earnings number sitting in your database today is often not the number the market saw on the reporting date. Companies restate, and most databases overwrite the original with the correction. Add filing lag, where the figure lived in the data before it was legally public. Put together: **your backtest is quietly trading on information from the future.** A screen on last quarter's EPS reads the republished value, not the one known that day. The fix is point-in-time data: the value as it was knowable that morning, not as the database shows it now.
cards.depth: Why it bites again: look-ahead bias does not announce itself. The strategy looks clean and the Sharpe looks real, because the leak is baked into the inputs, not the logic. Every fundamental backtest you run inherits it unless the data vendor stamps each value with the date it was actually knowable.

cards.hook: Delta flatters you. It overstates your odds twice.
cards.body: Traders read a 0.30 delta as a 30% chance the option finishes in the money. It isn't. Delta equals N(d1) in Black-Scholes, but the risk-neutral probability of expiring in the money is N(d2), which is always smaller. So **delta overstates even the risk-neutral odds**. Then a second gap opens: implied vol usually runs above realized, so the contract prices in a bigger move than the stock tends to make. The real-world probability sits below the risk-neutral one. Both errors push the same way, making your short strike feel safer than it reads.
cards.depth: The practical read: when you sell a 16-delta strangle, your actual odds of expiring outside the strikes are a touch better than 84%, because the variance risk premium is on your side. When you buy delta hoping it pays off, that same premium quietly works against you. Same number, opposite sign, depending on which side you take.

cards.hook: In a waterfall, recoupment order beats the headline split.
cards.body: Negotiators burn their energy on the percentage split of net proceeds. The bigger lever is **who recoups first, and how fast**. Money flows top down through the waterfall: senior recoupment, then fees, then the splits. A party sitting in a junior tier only sees dollars if the pool survives everything stacked above it, which on most projects it never does. A 50% split of a tier that stays dry is worth zero. A 20% split that sits above a guaranteed recoupment is worth real cash. Position in the stack is the term. The split is the decoration.
cards.depth: This is why sharp counsel trade split points for a better recoupment position or a first-dollar corridor. A corridor carves a slice off the top before senior recoupment, so you get paid even on a project that technically loses money. Winning the percentage while ceding the position is the classic rookie giveaway.

cards.hook: The rule that built indie TV, then streaming undid it.
cards.body: In 1970 the FCC adopted the **Financial Interest and Syndication Rules**, called fin-syn. They barred the three broadcast networks from owning financial stakes in, or syndicating, most of the primetime shows they aired. The networks could rent airtime but not own the library or the lucrative rerun rights. That forced a split between distribution and ownership, and it seeded a thriving independent studio economy that produced and owned the hits. By the mid-1990s the rules were gone. Ownership and distribution fused back together, and the studio-network mergers of the next decade followed directly from that opening.
cards.depth: The rhyme is loud. Streamers now own the pipe and the library at once, the exact concentration fin-syn was built to prevent. The difference is that no rule stops them, so leverage has swung back to whoever controls distribution. Creators pushing for backend ownership today are fighting the same vertical-integration fight, minus the referee.

cards.hook: You won't remember to remember. Bolt it to a habit.
cards.body: The failure is rarely forgetting what to do. It is **prospective memory**, the job of spontaneously retrieving an intention at the right future moment with no prompt. ADHD hits this hard, because self-initiated retrieval leans on exactly the executive function that runs weak. A mental note and a dose of willpower both lose to it. The move is to stop asking your brain to generate the cue. Anchor the new action to an existing, unavoidable one: take the pill when the coffee starts brewing, send the invoice the moment you sit down Monday. The habit you already have becomes the alarm.
cards.depth: This is why a reminder app often fails while a sticky note on the steering wheel works. The app fires on a schedule you have already tuned out. The anchor fires on an action you cannot skip, so the cue lives out in the world, not in the part of your head that keeps dropping it.

cards.hook: Recall it: your gut says two weeks. What question beats it?
cards.body: Your inside view builds the estimate from the specifics of this project, step by step, and it comes out too optimistic almost every time. The fix is the outside view: **ask how long similar projects actually took**, then start from that base rate. This is reference-class forecasting. You find the class of comparable efforts, take their real distribution of outcomes, and anchor on it before adjusting for anything genuinely unusual about yours. The reference class already knows about the delays you cannot yet see.
cards.depth: The planning fallacy is not a motivation problem, it is a sampling problem. Your own plan carries no record of the interruptions, scope creep, and plain bad luck that hit every project before it. Their finished timelines do. Trust the record over the story you are telling yourself.

cards.hook: Implied volatility is a biased forecast. That bias is your premium.
cards.body: Everyone treats implied volatility as the market's forecast of future movement. It isn't a clean one. Across S&P index options, implied vol has historically run above the volatility that actually prints, roughly three to four vol points on average over long samples. That persistent gap is the variance risk premium, and it is why systematically selling options carries an edge independent of direction. **You are paid to insure other people against moves that, on average, are smaller than priced.** The premium is the bias itself, not a mispricing you have to predict.
cards.depth: The caveat: the premium is compensation for real tail risk, not free money. It is largest exactly when it should scare you, and it goes negative in the crashes that wipe out naive sellers. Harvesting it is a bet on surviving the fat left tail, sized accordingly.

cards.hook: Tennessee made distributing a voice-clone tool its own offense.
cards.body: Tennessee's ELVIS Act (Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act) took effect July 1, 2024, and it did something federal copyright can't: it made voice an explicit, protectable property right. The part practitioners skip is the liability hook. The statute reaches anyone who makes available a tool or service whose primary purpose is producing an unauthorized replica of a specific artist's voice. **You can be liable without ever publishing a single fake.** Distributing the cloning tool is itself the actionable act. For a client building voice-AI, that shifts the exposure from the output to the product.
cards.depth: Why it matters now: most AI-liability analysis still fixates on the generated clip and asks whether a given output infringes. The ELVIS Act moves the risk upstream to the tool, which is a different diligence question and a different insurance conversation than output review.

cards.hook: Assume the plan already failed. You'll find more reasons why.
cards.body: A premortem, from Gary Klein, flips the question before you commit. Instead of asking 'what could go wrong,' you assume the plan has already failed a year from now and work backward to explain why. The change is grammatical, and that is the whole trick. **Stating the failure as a fact unlocks concrete causes that a hypothetical never surfaces.** The research, reported in late-1980s work on prospective hindsight, found roughly a 30% increase in the number of reasons people could generate. Certainty of failure is a sharper search prompt than mere possibility.
cards.depth: It pairs with resulting, the habit of grading a decision by how it happened to turn out. A premortem forces you to price the failure paths while the odds are still in front of you, so a later bad draw doesn't look like a surprise you should have seen.

cards.hook: Your internal clock is broken. Make time take up space.
cards.body: Time blindness is a measurable deficit, not a character flaw: the ADHD brain poorly represents how much time has elapsed or how much remains. You cannot will the internal clock into working, so the move is to stop relying on it. **Externalize time into something spatial you can see.** A depleting visual timer, like the shrinking colored disc of a Time Timer, turns an invisible quantity into a shape that visibly contracts in your field of view. The point is passive glanceability: you read remaining time without stopping to query it, because that query is the one that never happens.
cards.depth: This is why a number on a phone fails for this brain: it requires an act of checking, and checking is the executive step that drops out. A shape simply sitting in view removes the decision. Put it up before you start the task, not when you notice you've already lost the thread.

cards.hook: Recall it: your backtest looks brilliant. Which names are missing?
cards.body: You pulled today's stock universe and ran the strategy back twenty years. Give it a beat before the answer. Every name on that list is one that didn't go bankrupt, get delisted, or get bought at a loss. The losers were deleted from the data, not from history. That is **survivorship bias**, and it is why a long-biased system looks like genius against a universe scrubbed of its own failures. Your strategy never had to hold the ones that went to zero. The fix is a point-in-time database that still carries the dead.
cards.depth: Worth re-flagging because it stacks with the other sins. Survivorship inflates the return curve first, then you overfit to that inflated curve, so two biases compound. Any backtest built on a universe you sourced today is suspect before you even look at the Sharpe.

cards.hook: Long gamma pays you to rebalance. That's the edge.
cards.body: A delta-hedged long option is **long gamma**: when the stock rises your delta climbs, so you sell shares into the move; when it falls your delta drops, so you buy. Every oscillation forces you to sell high and buy low, and you book the difference. The position harvests the stock's realized movement one re-hedge at a time. You pay theta each day for the right to keep scalping. It wins only when realized volatility, summed across all those hedges, beats the implied volatility you paid at entry.
cards.depth: This is why a long straddle can bleed to zero in a quiet market even if the stock eventually gaps. The path between your hedges, not the final price, is what pays. Set the re-hedge band too wide and you miss the scalp; too narrow and transaction costs eat it alive.

cards.hook: Training on the books was fair use. Getting them wasn't.
cards.body: In **Bartz v. Anthropic**, a federal judge ruled that using copyrighted books to train a model was transformative fair use. But the same opinion held that downloading pirated copies to build the training library was ordinary infringement, fair use or not. The lesson practitioners keep missing: how you acquired the data is a separate claim from how you used it. A clean fair-use defense on the output does nothing for a tainted-provenance claim on the inputs. The case reportedly settled for roughly $1.5 billion on the acquisition side.
cards.depth: It splits the AI-copyright question in two. 'Was the use transformative?' is the headline fight, but 'did you have the right to possess the copy you learned from?' is the quieter and often stronger claim. Scraped-from-the-open-web and bought-then-pirated sit very differently on that second axis.

cards.hook: Rebound fools you into chasing a higher dose.
cards.body: As a long-acting stimulant like **lisdexamfetamine** clears, blood levels can dip below baseline for a stretch before settling. That rebound window feels like inattention roaring back, which tempts a dose increase when the real fix is timing. The mechanism: the medication effect tracks the blood-level curve, and the tail of that curve is predictable. The move is to schedule your highest-activation work, the thing you most dread starting, inside the peak window, and leave the fading tail for low-stakes or already-running tasks. Do not start the hard thing at 4 p.m.
cards.depth: Titration is partly about finding the dose, but just as much about mapping your own curve: note when focus arrives, when it peaks, when it fades. That map, not the milligram number alone, tells you where to put the work that needs the most push to begin.

cards.hook: Your 90% confident range is wrong about half the time.
cards.body: Ask people for a range they are **90% sure** contains the true answer, and the right answer falls outside it far more than 10 percent of the time. Reported hit rates in calibration studies cluster around 40 to 50 percent. The mechanism is anchoring: you fix on a best guess, then nudge the edges out too timidly, so your 'wide' range is still built around your point estimate. The fix is mechanical. Set your interval, then widen it until it feels absurd, because absurd is usually where calibrated actually lives.
cards.depth: This is why a trader sizing to a 'worst case' still gets wrecked, and why a lawyer's 'range of outcomes' misses the tail. The failure is not ignorance of the number; it is false precision about how well you know it. Track your own intervals for a month and you can measure your true hit rate.

cards.hook: Recall it: caffeine blocks the alarm. What keeps piling up?
cards.body: **Adenosine.** Across waking hours it accumulates in the brain and binds the receptors that signal sleep pressure. Caffeine works by blocking those receptors, so you stop feeling the pressure, but the adenosine keeps building the entire time. When the caffeine clears, all of it is still there and binds at once. That is the crash. The debt was never paid down, only hidden, and the only thing that truly clears adenosine is sleep.
cards.depth: Practical read: caffeine late in the day blocks receptors for hours, since its half-life runs several hours, so it can blunt the very pressure you need to fall asleep and deepen tomorrow's deficit. Timing beats dose.

cards.hook: A stock pinned to your strike is a Monday-morning mystery.
cards.body: Expiration lands with the underlying sitting almost exactly on your short strike. Now you have a problem: whether you get assigned depends on whether the long holder chooses to exercise, and at a penny in or out of the money that choice is unpredictable. So you can go home Friday thinking you're flat and wake up Monday unexpectedly long or short 100 shares per contract, carrying a full weekend of unhedged gap risk. **Pin risk is uncertainty about your position, not your price.** Market makers hedge hard into the close precisely to avoid being caught naked by it.
cards.depth: It bites worst in low-priced, heavily-optioned names where huge open interest clusters at round strikes, and dealer hedging can actually drag the price toward that strike into the bell. The fix is boring: close or roll a near-the-money short before expiration rather than hoping it settles clean.

cards.hook: The Warhol ruling quietly reshaped every AI fair-use defense.
cards.body: Practitioners still reach for the Google Books era, when 'the machine learned something new' made a use transformative and factor one fell their way. Warhol v. Goldsmith (2023) narrowed that. The Supreme Court held the first factor weighs a use's purpose against its commercial character and whether it serves the **same market** as the original. Applied to AI, learning from a work is not automatically transformative if the output competes with that work. The question shifted from 'is it new?' to 'does it substitute?'
cards.depth: That is why factor four, market harm, is now the real battleground in the training-data suits, and why the Meta authors' loss turned largely on failing to prove the market they were denied. A defense built on pre-2023 transformativeness language is quietly out of date.

cards.hook: More detail made it feel likelier. Which rule does that break?
cards.body: Picture Linda: thoughtful, outspoken, once a philosophy major. Is she more likely a bank teller, or a bank teller who is also a feminist? Most people pick the second, which is impossible, since every feminist bank teller is already a bank teller. The answer is the **conjunction rule**: P(A and B) can never exceed P(A). Adding a vivid, fitting detail raises a scenario's plausibility while it can only lower its probability. The richer story is the weaker bet.
cards.depth: This is the one to keep live at the screen. When a forecast or a thesis arrives fully furnished with reasons, treat each added clause as another condition that must independently come true. The clean, under-specified version is usually the better odds.

cards.hook: Make the first step too small to refuse.
cards.body: Starting carries a fixed activation cost, and the ADHD brain overweights it, so a task labeled 'write the report' triggers avoidance long before any writing would happen. The size of the step you picture is what your brain prices, not the size of the job. **Shrink the entry point below the threshold:** not 'write the report' but 'open the file and type one bad sentence.' Once you are moving, continuation is cheap, because the expensive part was always the standing start, not the run.
cards.depth: This is why 'just do five minutes' works and 'buckle down' doesn't. Five minutes is a step small enough to clear the threshold; buckling down is a mountain your brain refuses to price. Size the first move, not the willpower.

cards.hook: An MFN you grant can handcuff every future deal.
cards.body: A most-favored-nations clause promises your counterparty they will automatically get any better term you later hand someone else. Granting it feels free, because on signing day it costs nothing. The mechanism that bites shows up later: it **strips your ability to price-discriminate.** You can no longer give a bigger, more valuable partner a sweeter deal without retroactively upgrading the MFN holder too, so the clause quietly caps the upside of every negotiation that follows it.
cards.depth: The real fights are over scope. Is it compared term-by-term or whole-deal? Which terms count as 'comparable'? Does it reach deals struck by affiliates, or only you? A narrow, term-matched MFN with affiliate carve-outs is survivable; a broad whole-deal one gives away your future leverage.

cards.hook: A covered call is a short put wearing a disguise.
cards.body: Put-call parity forces it. Long stock plus a short call at strike K has the exact same payoff as a short put at K, same expiry: identical P&L curve, identical downside, identical breakeven. The covered call feels conservative because you own the shares, but all the risk lives in the stock you hold, and the call caps upside the way a short put does. **The only real differences are margin treatment and assignment mechanics, not risk.** If you would never naked-short the put, the covered call is that same bet with better optics.
cards.depth: This is why 'safe income' covered-call funds are selling puts in all but name. The premium you collect is the same variance risk premium a put seller earns, and your worst case, stock to zero minus premium, matches the put seller's exactly.

cards.hook: A reward next week barely exists to your brain today.
cards.body: The mechanism is steep delay discounting. A reward's motivational pull decays with time-to-payoff far faster in an ADHD reward system, so a deadline that is seven days out generates almost no signal now, no matter how much it will matter then. Willpower does not fix this; it is a valuation problem, not a character one. The move is to **manufacture a near-term stake the task can actually compete with**: a same-day checkpoint, a visible checkmark, a text you owe someone by 5p, money on the line tonight. Pull the payoff into today or nothing fires.
cards.depth: This is also why external deadlines beat internal ones for you. An internal 'I should finish this week' sits on the flat, discounted part of the curve; a real consequence due today sits on the steep part where motivation actually lives.

cards.hook: The first training case lost fair use, and it wasn't generative.
cards.body: In February 2025, Judge Bibas handed Thomson Reuters the first real win against AI training. Ross Intelligence had copied Westlaw's editorial headnotes to build a competing legal-research tool. Bibas, reversing his own earlier view, held the use was not fair. Two factors decided it: the purpose was **not transformative because Ross wasn't generative**, it was assembling a direct market substitute, and the fourth factor, market harm, pointed hard at Thomson Reuters because Ross aimed at its customers. The takeaway practitioners drew: non-generative copying plus direct competition is the losing combination.
cards.depth: Most generative-AI defendants will argue precisely what Ross couldn't, that their output is transformative and serves a different market. Bibas drew that line explicitly, which is why the ruling cut against Ross while handing the OpenAIs and Metas a distinction to stand on.

cards.hook: Your fundamentals backtest knows numbers that didn't exist yet.
cards.body: Companies restate earnings, and most databases overwrite the original figure with the corrected one. So a strategy that screens on last quarter's EPS is often reading the number as republished months later, not the number the market actually saw on the reporting date. Add filing lag, the data existed in the database before it was legally public, and your backtest is quietly trading on information from the future. **Use point-in-time data: the value as it was known that day, not as the database shows it now.** Otherwise you are grading hindsight.
cards.depth: It is a sneakier cousin of survivorship bias. There the row is missing entirely; here the row is present but holds the wrong value, so the backtest looks complete and clean while being contaminated in every cell you restated.

cards.hook: Superforecasters beat the experts. What was their actual edge?
cards.body: Not raw intelligence, not better sources, not access. Think about what they did differently every time a new fact landed... They broke questions into parts, started from base rates, then **updated in small, frequent increments** as evidence arrived. The ordinary forecaster anchors on a first guess and lurches in rare, dramatic jumps. The winner nudges 60 to 63 on real news and beats the one who leaps 50 to 90 on a hunch and then freezes for a month. The skill is granular updating, not the opening call.
cards.depth: Worth re-filing because your trading version is identical: the loss is refusing to move a thesis one notch when a single piece of evidence lands, then overcorrecting hard later. Update often, update small, and the first number matters less than you think.

cards.hook: A deep in-the-money put gets exercised early for interest.
cards.body: Everyone learns that an American call is exercised early only to capture a dividend. The mirror case for puts gets skipped. A holder of a deep in-the-money put can exercise to collect the strike in cash now and earn interest on it. The remaining time value that far in the money is tiny, so the interest on the strike can exceed it. **The driver is the time value of money, not volatility.** If you are short that put, early assignment is the risk you never priced.
cards.depth: The symmetry is clean. Calls pay you to wait unless a dividend makes holding the stock worth more now. Puts pay you to wait unless interest on the strike makes cash-in-hand worth more now. Higher rates widen the window where early put exercise is rational, which is why it was routine in high-rate decades and nearly vanished near zero.

cards.hook: Regurgitation is the plaintiff's best exhibit in an AI suit.
cards.body: Training on copyrighted text may be fair use. Producing a near-verbatim copy of that text is a different problem, and plaintiffs know it. **The strongest evidence in the training-data cases is memorization**: a prompt that makes the model spit back long passages close to the original. The New York Times complaint against OpenAI leaned on exactly this, showing article text the model reproduced. It bridges the gap between 'trained on my work' and 'copied my work,' which is the gap defendants most want to keep open. Expect every complaint to go hunting for it.
cards.depth: Why it matters: fair use turns partly on market harm and the amount taken. Verbatim output is hard to sell as transformative and reads as a substitute for the original. It also reframes the case from an abstract training theory, which courts treat skeptically, into ordinary copying, which they understand. The engineering fix, output filters that block regurgitation, is itself a quiet admission the risk is real.

cards.hook: Every task switch reloads working memory, your weakest part.
cards.body: Switching tasks is not free. Each switch forces your brain to drop the current context and reload the next one, and that reload lives in working memory. For an ADHD brain, working memory is the constrained resource, so the switch tax lands harder and the dropped context is harder to recover. **The move is to batch by mode, not by project.** Answer every email in one block, make every call in another. You are not saving time on the tasks themselves. You are paying the reload tax once instead of fifteen times.
cards.depth: The hidden version is the 'quick check' of a phone or inbox mid-task. It feels like seconds, but it evicts the context you were holding and forces a full reload when you come back. The cost is not the thirty seconds on the phone. It is the two minutes rebuilding where you were, every single time.

cards.hook: Your backtest only trades the companies that survived.
cards.body: Pull a universe of stocks as it exists today, backtest a strategy over the last twenty years, and you have already cheated. The names on that list are the ones that did not go bankrupt, get delisted, or get bought at a loss. **The losers were deleted from the data, not from history.** Your strategy never had to hold the ones that went to zero, because they are not in the file. A long-biased system looks brilliant against a universe scrubbed of its own failures. The fix is a point-in-time database that still includes the dead.
cards.depth: This is why index backtests overstate returns, and why mean-reversion looks especially strong: buying the dip works beautifully until you buy a dip that keeps falling to zero, and survivorship bias has quietly removed every one of those. The same flaw hides in fund-performance studies, where closed and merged funds vanish and the survivors alone define the average.

cards.hook: You're estimating how long a project takes. What beats your gut?
cards.body: Think back a few days before the answer lands. The unreliable path reasons from your own plan and your reasons this time is special, and it runs optimistic because it cannot picture the failures it has not imagined yet. The better move is the **outside view**: ignore your specifics and ask how the reference class of similar efforts actually turned out. Define the class, get its distribution, then adjust only slightly for what is genuinely unique to you. Kahneman and Lovallo showed the base rate beats the confident inside story almost every time.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: it is the same engine behind a trading edge. Your setup feels special, but the honest prior is what that setup has paid across hundreds of past instances, not the story you are telling about this one. Inside view for the narrative, outside view for the number.

cards.hook: An at-the-money straddle prices the expected move.
cards.body: Buy the at-the-money call and put and you've bought a clean read on the market's expected move. The mechanism: an ATM straddle is worth **roughly 0.8 times the one-standard-deviation move** to expiry (about 0.8 x S x sigma x sqrt(T) in Black-Scholes, since each ATM leg runs near 0.4 x S x sigma x sqrt(T)). So a straddle quoted at 5% of spot implies a one-sigma move near 6%. Earnings desks trade the gap between that implied move and what actually prints, not the direction.
cards.depth: The 0.8 factor assumes a roughly normal distribution and an exactly at-the-money strike. Fat tails and heavy put skew pull it around, which is why desks calibrate the multiplier to each name rather than trusting the textbook number.

cards.hook: Judging a decision by its outcome is a bug.
cards.body: Annie Duke calls it **resulting**: grading the quality of a choice by how it happened to turn out. A good decision can lose and a reckless one can win, because the world runs on probability and you only ever see one draw. The fix is to keep two separate ledgers. Score the decision against what you knew and the odds you faced at the time. Score the outcome separately, as a single data point that updates your model. Conflate them and you abandon a sound process after one bad beat and double down on a lucky mistake.
cards.depth: This is why poker players and traders keep decision journals written before the result lands. The journal freezes your reasoning so you can audit the process without hindsight contaminating it. Outcome-only review quietly trains you to get more risk-averse after losses and more reckless after wins, which is exactly backwards.

cards.hook: Pre-decide the trigger, not just the task.
cards.body: Executive function is weakest at the moment of starting, when you have to both notice the cue and choose to act. An **implementation intention** collapses that into one step: a pre-written 'when X, then Y.' When my coffee is poured, I open the brief. When I sit at the desk, the first file is already on screen. The if-then fires on the cue without routing through the part of your brain that negotiates. You are not relying on remembering, or on wanting to. You have wired the start to something that already happens anyway.
cards.depth: Gollwitzer's studies found the effect largest exactly where self-regulation is hardest, which is the population you care about. Make the cue something already reliable in your day, not a new habit you also have to install. The failure mode is a vague cue like 'when I have time'; the cue has to be a specific, observable moment.

cards.hook: Training infringement and output infringement are two different suits.
cards.body: Practitioners keep blurring two claims that live on opposite ends of the model. **Input-side** is about copying works to build the training set; that is where the fair-use fights happen, and courts have split. **Output-side** is about whether a specific generation is substantially similar to a protected work, which is ordinary infringement and does not care how the model was trained. A model can win the training fight and still produce an infringing image. Advising a client, you scope both: how the thing was built, and, separately, what it spits out and how they use it.
cards.depth: The practical tell: an indemnity that only covers 'training data rights' leaves the client exposed on outputs, and the reverse leaves them exposed on inputs. Vendors increasingly offer output indemnities precisely because the training question is unsettled while the output question is old, familiar copyright law they can price.

cards.hook: Recall it: a decade of great returns. What did it learn?
cards.body: If a single backtest nailed 2010 to 2020, ask what it actually encoded. Often the answer is **the regime, not an edge**: a persistent bull, falling rates, one volatility environment. The strategy did not discover a durable relationship. It memorized the shape of a particular decade and will keep betting that shape forward. The test is regime slicing. Break the history into distinct environments (rates up vs down, high vs low vol, bull vs bear) and check whether the edge survives each one. An edge that only exists in one regime is just a bet that the regime continues.
cards.depth: This is the quiet cousin of overfitting. You did not torture the parameters; the market handed you one long, friendly environment and the backtest took the credit. A strategy that holds across regimes is rarer and far more valuable than one with a higher headline Sharpe in a single era.

cards.hook: A 25-delta put costs more than its mirror call.
cards.body: Equity index options show a persistent skew: out-of-the-money puts trade at higher implied vol than equidistant out-of-the-money calls. Two forces drive it. The leverage effect, where a falling stock's debt-to-equity rises and its volatility mechanically climbs, so down moves really are more volatile. And crash-o-phobia, the structural demand from hedgers who will overpay for downside protection. The result is that **skew is a risk premium you either harvest or pay**, depending on your side. Selling that rich put vol works right up until the crash it was priced for actually shows up.
cards.depth: Skew also makes your hedges asymmetric. The same move down changes your option's vol, not just its price, so a put seller is short both spot and the vol that spikes exactly when spot drops. That correlation is why short-put books unwind faster than their Greeks suggest on a calm day.

cards.hook: California voids a digital-replica clause if it's too vague.
cards.body: AB 2602, effective 2025, makes a performer's consent to an AI digital replica **unenforceable when the clause is too vague about how the replica will be used** and the performer signed without a lawyer or a union representative. A blanket grant covering all uses, all media, forever, the studio default, is exactly what fails. It bites where the replica would replace work the person would otherwise have done live. So the statute attacks the contract's specificity, not the technology. Breadth, usually the drafter's shield, becomes the weakness here.
cards.depth: This inverts normal drafting instinct. Ordinarily the broadest grant protects the buyer. Here breadth is the exposure: a court can strike the clause for vagueness and leave a producer holding footage with no license behind it. The defensive move is narrow, enumerated, use-by-use consent, which is the opposite of how rights usually get papered.

cards.hook: Every added detail makes a forecast feel likelier and be less likely.
cards.body: The conjunction rule is just arithmetic: the probability of A and B can never exceed the probability of A alone. Yet add a vivid, coherent detail to a prediction and people rate the fuller story as more probable, not less. Kahneman and Tversky's Linda problem found most respondents judged 'bank teller and feminist' more likely than 'bank teller,' which is impossible. For a forecaster the lesson is sharp: **specificity buys plausibility at the cost of probability**. The rich, convincing scenario is usually the one to bet against, because every clause you add is one more condition that has to come true.
cards.depth: This bites hardest in deal and trade theses. The compelling narrative, clean mechanism, named catalyst, feels like the strong call. But it has stacked conjunctions, and each one multiplies the others downward. The vaguer, uglier 'something breaks' thesis often carries the higher true probability.

cards.hook: Your new system didn't fail. Its novelty did.
cards.body: Every productivity system you adopt works beautifully for about two weeks, then quietly dies. The usual read is a discipline failure. The mechanism is narrower: the system ran on **novelty-driven interest, not on habit**, and ADHD attention is powered by interest, not importance. When the newness wears off, the dopamine that was carrying adherence stops, and the system has no fuel left. Willpower was never holding it up. The move is to expect the decay and design around it: rotate tools before they go stale, or build the system so it runs without needing your attention to stay alive.
cards.depth: This is why 'just use a planner' advice fails on repeat. The planner is not the problem, the expectation of permanence is. A tool that survives is usually one that got automated, handed to someone else, or rebuilt often enough that each version is briefly novel again. Plan the replacement before you need it.

cards.hook: Recall it: what does the in-sample minus walk-forward Sharpe gap measure?
cards.body: Think back to the method that trades only unseen slices. One backtest fit over all of history just measures how well you explained a past you already knew happened. Walk-forward refits on a rolling window and trades the next slice it has never seen, again and again, so the P&L you keep is out-of-sample by construction. The answer: **the gap between the in-sample Sharpe and the walk-forward Sharpe is the honest size of your overfit**. A small gap points to real structure. A large gap means you curve-fit a story onto noise.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: a single flattering equity curve gives you no gap to look at, so nothing ever warns you. Walk-forward forces the comparison into existence. Run only one backtest and you have thrown away the one diagnostic that tells you whether the edge is real or imagined.

cards.hook: Long gamma always costs theta. Convexity is never free.
cards.body: Buy an option and you own positive gamma: the position improves as the underlying moves either way. But you pay for that curvature every day in theta. The link is mechanical. For a given implied volatility, the gamma you hold fixes the decay you bleed, dollar for dollar. So being long options is never a free bet on a big move. **You win only if realized movement outruns the implied vol you paid.** Direction barely matters; the whole trade is realized versus implied.
cards.depth: This is why gamma scalping is a volatility trade, not a directional one. You delta-hedge to strip out direction and harvest the gap between how much the underlying actually moves and how much its options priced in. Positive when realized beats implied, negative when it lags.

cards.hook: A voice can't be copyrighted. Bette Midler still won.
cards.body: In 1988 Midler sued Ford for hiring a sound-alike to imitate her recording. Copyright didn't help, since she didn't own the song and they used a different singer. She won anyway, on California's right of publicity: a distinctive voice is part of identity, and imitating it to sell a product is misappropriation. Tom Waits later beat Frito-Lay the same way. **AI voice clones inherit this framework, not copyright.** The winning theory against a cloned voice is publicity and unfair competition, because the voice itself was never copyrightable subject matter.
cards.depth: That is why the recent statutes, Tennessee's ELVIS Act and California's replica laws, extend publicity rights rather than copyright. They target the unauthorized use of identity. A practitioner drafting AI clauses should protect the voice as identity, not as a work, and lean on state publicity law where copyright has nothing to grab.

cards.hook: Superforecasters don't predict better. They update more often.
cards.body: Tetlock's forecasting tournaments found the top performers weren't smarter or better informed. Their edge was process: they broke questions into pieces, started from base rates, then adjusted in small, frequent increments as news arrived. Ordinary forecasters anchor on a first guess and move in rare, dramatic leaps. **The skill is granular updating, not the initial call.** A forecaster who nudges from 60% to 63% on real evidence beats one who jumps 50% to 90% on a hunch and then freezes for a month.
cards.depth: The trading parallel is exact. A thesis is a starting probability, not a commitment. Each earnings print, each tape reaction is an update, and the discipline is sizing the move to the evidence. Big convictions that never revise are how good analysts blow up.

cards.hook: Stuck on a task? Change the room, not the plan.
cards.body: Novelty spikes dopamine, and an under-stimulated reward system disengages fastest from the stale and familiar. That's why a task you've stared at for an hour feels impossible, while the same task at a different desk suddenly moves. You're not fixing motivation; you're handing a novelty-hungry system a fresh context to latch onto. **Rotate the environment to reset engagement, not the workload.** A cafe, another room, even facing a different wall can restart a stalled task without changing one thing about the work itself.
cards.depth: Same reason changing the task's surface helps: a new font, reading it aloud, switching from screen to paper. The novelty is doing the work, not the medium. Reach for it deliberately and cheaply before you reach for willpower or a second dose.

cards.hook: Recall it: 20 strategies tested, best kept. Why distrust its Sharpe?
cards.body: Answer: multiple-testing bias. Search enough variations and one will look brilliant by luck alone. Test 20 strategies and, even if none has real edge, the best backtest posts a Sharpe that looks significant, because you selected on noise. The more you tried, the higher that lucky peak climbs. **The number of things you tested is part of the result, and it usually gets hidden.** The fix is the deflated Sharpe ratio, which discounts the winner by how many candidates you searched to find it.
cards.depth: It is different from overfitting one model. Here each strategy might be honestly built, yet choosing the best of many inflates the result on its own. Report how many you tried, or hold out data you never touched during the search.

cards.hook: A hedged option's daily P&L is a bet on one gap.
cards.body: When you delta-hedge a short option, the day's profit collapses to the gap between the volatility you sold and the volatility that shows up, scaled by gamma. Sell at 20 and the stock realizes 15, you keep the difference; it realizes 28 and you bleed. Once hedged, the position stops caring about direction and starts caring only about **how much the stock actually moves versus what you sold**. That is why selling options is called trading realized against implied: the strike and the drift wash out, and one variance comparison, repeated daily, is the entire game.
cards.depth: The scaling term is dollar gamma, so the same volatility miss hurts far more near the strike and near expiry, where gamma spikes. A position that looks calm for weeks can take its whole loss in the last few pinning days. Hedge too rarely and your realized-vol capture itself turns noisy.

cards.hook: The authors lost to Meta by arguing the wrong harm.
cards.body: In June 2025 Judge Chhabria ruled for Meta in the authors' training-data suit, but the opinion read like a warning shot. He said the plaintiffs lost mainly because they leaned on the copying itself and barely argued **market dilution**: that a model can flood the market with cheap, similar books and gut demand for the originals. On that theory, he suggested, many AI companies could lose. The fight practitioners now see coming has migrated from 'did you copy the inputs' to 'does the output destroy the market those inputs served.'
cards.depth: This splits from Judge Alsup's Anthropic ruling issued days earlier in the same district, which treated training as strongly transformative and downplayed dilution. Two judges, opposite emphasis, means the fourth fair-use factor, market effect, is now the contested ground, and future plaintiffs will plead dilution from the first filing.

cards.hook: A precise first offer anchors harder than a round one.
cards.body: Anchoring research keeps finding that first offers drag the final price toward them, but the subtler result is about precision. Open at $9,800 and you tend to hold more ground than opening at $10,000. The precise number signals you have **specific information behind it**, so the other side assumes your true number is close and makes smaller counter-adjustments. Round figures read as placeholders and invite round-number haggling in big jumps. The move in a deal you know cold: anchor first, anchor precisely, and let the specificity imply diligence you never have to fully spell out.
cards.depth: The effect has limits. Wildly precise anchors on a genuinely fuzzy asset read as false precision and cost credibility. And precision only pays if you actually open first. Ceding the first number to seem reasonable usually just hands the anchor, and the whole adjustment advantage, to the other side.

cards.hook: Caffeine hides sleep pressure. It doesn't drain it.
cards.body: Adenosine builds in the brain every waking hour and is the molecule that makes you feel tired: your **sleep pressure gauge**. Caffeine works by plugging adenosine's receptors so the signal can't land, which is why you feel alert, not because the pressure is gone. Adenosine keeps piling up behind the block. When the caffeine clears, all of it binds at once, and that is the crash. Caffeine's half-life runs roughly five to six hours, so a 3 p.m. coffee still has about a quarter of its dose working near 1 a.m.
cards.depth: This is why afternoon caffeine wrecks sleep quality even when you fall asleep fine: it suppresses slow-wave sleep, so you clear less adenosine overnight and wake with residual pressure, reaching for more. The loop feeds itself. Front-loading caffeine before noon is what breaks it.

cards.hook: Recall it: why did praising pilots seem to backfire?
cards.body: Think back to the flight instructors who swore that praising a good landing ruined the next one and chewing out a bad one improved it. What single statistical force produced both illusions, with no causal effect from anything they said? Give it a beat. **Regression to the mean.** An exceptional landing is partly luck, so the next drifts back toward average, meaning worse; a terrible one drifts back toward better. They read a mechanical bounce as a response to their feedback and learned exactly the wrong lesson about people.
cards.depth: It matters again at your P&L. Your best month and worst month both partly regress next month, so 'what did I change after the bad stretch' quietly collects false credit for a rebound that was coming anyway. Judge the process, not the swing that was always going to fade.

cards.hook: Shorting vol pays twice: the premium and the roll.
cards.body: The VIX futures curve usually slopes upward in calm markets. A future priced above spot must fall toward spot as expiration nears, all else equal. If you are short that future, that decay is money even if realized volatility never changes. This is **roll yield**, and in quiet regimes it can dwarf the raw variance premium. The catch is symmetry: when the curve inverts in a panic the same roll works violently against you, and it inverts exactly when you are already bleeding on the spot move.
cards.depth: Contango-to-backwardation flips are fast and correlated with the drawdown itself. That is why short-vol curves show long calm stretches punctuated by cliffs. The roll is not free carry. It is compensation for agreeing to hold the crash when it comes.

cards.hook: Whether AI can resurrect you depends on where you died.
cards.body: Right of publicity has no federal statute. It is a **state-by-state patchwork**, and the state that governs is usually the performer's domicile at death, not where the ad runs. California and Tennessee recognize robust post-mortem rights lasting decades. New York only recently added a 40-year post-mortem digital-replica right for performers. Several states recognize no descendible right at all. So a synthetic performance of a dead actor can be lawful or actionable based purely on the estate's chosen home. Talent estates now plan domicile the way the wealthy plan trusts.
cards.depth: This is why AI-resurrection clauses increasingly specify governing law and the performer's declared domicile rather than leaning on the forum of production. Estates that want protection migrate toward California or Tennessee; those that do not can stay exposed no matter how the deal reads. The choice-of-law fight is the ballgame.

cards.hook: Don't ask how long this will take. Ask how long they took.
cards.body: The **inside view** builds an estimate from the specifics of your case: your plan, your team, your reasons this time is different. It runs optimistic because it cannot see the failures it has not imagined yet. The outside view ignores your details and asks a base-rate question instead: how did the reference class of similar efforts actually turn out? Kahneman and Lovallo argued the outside view routinely beats the confident inside estimate. The move is mechanical. Define the class, get its distribution, then adjust only slightly for what is genuinely unique to you.
cards.depth: The failure mode is picking a flattering class of one. 'Projects like mine' quietly becomes 'my best project.' Force the class wider than feels fair, count the disasters honestly, and let the distribution, not the story, anchor the number you commit to.

cards.hook: Take the pill 90 minutes before the task, not at it.
cards.body: Lisdexamfetamine is a **prodrug**: it is inactive until your body cleaves off the lysine and releases the active stimulant. That conversion is gradual, so meaningful effect builds over roughly one to two hours after you swallow it, not on contact. The practical move is to dose against your hardest activation window, not the moment you sit down. If the wall you avoid is 9 a.m. email, taking it at 9 means you fight the wall unmedicated and peak after the morning is already gone. Front-load the clock instead.
cards.depth: This also explains the flat, gradual feel versus immediate-release stimulants, and why rushing it changes little: the rate limit is enzymatic, not about dose size. Pair the timing with a fixed wake anchor so the curve lands in the same place every day.

cards.hook: Recall it: why separate the checker from the writer?
cards.body: A model grading its own fresh output tends to ratify it. The same context, the same assumptions, and the same blind spots that produced the answer also approve it. **Separation forces independence.** A checker spun up as its own call, without the writer's reasoning in context, has to reconstruct the judgment from the artifact alone, and that is exactly when errors surface. Give it a narrow question and the original spec, not the writer's chain of thought. That is why review is a different call, not a polite second paragraph tacked onto the same one.
cards.depth: The trap is passing the writer's reasoning into the checker to 'save tokens.' That reintroduces the very shared context you were trying to break, and the check quietly becomes a rubber stamp. Fresh eyes means fresh context: the artifact, the spec, and nothing else.

cards.hook: Short options aren't one bet. Near-term risks moves, long-term risks repricing.
cards.body: Selling a weekly and selling a LEAPS both collect premium, but the risk you're actually short is different. **Short-dated options carry most of their risk in gamma**: a sharp move over the next few days can gut you before implied vol even twitches. Long-dated options carry it in vega: the position bleeds when the market simply reprices volatility higher, even with the underlying flat. A front-month seller loses to realized moves. A LEAPS seller loses to a vol-regime shift. Match the tenor to whichever risk you can actually stomach and hedge.
cards.depth: The rule of thumb: gamma scales inversely with time to expiry while vega scales with roughly its square root. So the near-dated book whipsaws on price and the long-dated book whipsaws on the vol surface. Two different Greeks, two different hedges, one premium check.

cards.hook: SAG-AFTRA split digital replicas into two kinds. Consent differs.
cards.body: The 2023 SAG-AFTRA TV/theatrical contract created two categories most coverage flattens into one. An **Employment-Based Digital Replica** is a scan made during a job you were hired for. An Independently Created Digital Replica is built from pre-existing footage outside that employment. Both require consent, but the consent and payment terms differ, and the replica can't be dropped into other productions without a fresh deal. The practitioner error is treating any signed AI clause as blanket permission. Which replica, made when, for what use, is the whole negotiation.
cards.depth: The consent also has to be specific: it must describe the replica's intended use with enough particularity that a general 'we may use your likeness with AI' grant sits closer to unenforceable than airtight. Specificity is the load-bearing term here, same as in every likeness license.

cards.hook: A 90%-accurate test, a positive result, and your odds are 8%.
cards.body: Take a condition that affects 1 in 100 people and a test that's 90% accurate both ways. You test positive. Most people, including doctors in the classic 1978 studies, guess the odds near 90%. The real answer is **about 8%**. Out of 1,000 people, 10 are sick and about 9 test positive. But 990 are healthy, and roughly 99 of them test positive falsely. Ninety-nine false alarms swamp nine true ones. The base rate, not the test's accuracy, drives the answer. Same trap in every 'strong signal' that fires against a rare event.
cards.depth: For a trader or a lawyer this is the alarm-fatigue math: a rare event plus an imperfect detector produces mostly false positives, no matter how sharp the detector sounds. To move the posterior you need a rarer false-positive rate or independent confirming evidence, not one louder signal.

cards.hook: A silent witness lowers the cost of starting.
cards.body: Body doubling means doing your task while another person is simply present, in the room or on a video call, not helping, just there. It reliably lowers activation cost for ADHD brains, and the mechanism isn't willpower. **A present observer adds external accountability and a small arousal bump**, two things an under-stimulated brain can't manufacture alone for a boring task. The task hasn't changed. The context around it has. The concrete move: schedule the dull thing with a witness. A coworking call, a friend on mute, a parent in the kitchen. Presence is the intervention.
cards.depth: It's why the same person who can't start a form alone finishes it in a cafe. Not the caffeine: the ambient social presence supplies the salience and mild self-monitoring the task itself fails to trigger. You're externalizing accountability, the same way you'd externalize the next step onto a sticky note.

cards.hook: Recall it: a great backtest, worthless at scale. What broke?
cards.body: Think back before the answer lands. A signal that printed beautiful returns on a small book can be worthless on a large one, and the culprit isn't the edge. It's **market impact**: your own orders eat liquidity and push the price against you, and the cost grows roughly with the square root of your order as a fraction of daily volume. So ten times the size is more than ten times the cost. The backtest filled at the quote and never charged you for moving it. Capacity, not raw edge, decides whether it survives real money.
cards.depth: Why it matters again: every impressive small-account result carries an invisible capacity ceiling. Before sizing up, ask what fraction of daily volume your fills represent, then re-run the numbers with a square-root cost term added. The edge that dies on contact with real money usually dies right here.

cards.hook: The only reason to exercise a call early is the dividend.
cards.body: An American call on a non-dividend stock is never worth exercising early. Selling it always beats exercising, because you keep the remaining time value and defer paying the strike. The one exception is a dividend. When the payout exceeds the interest earned on the strike plus the call's remaining time value, exercising the day before the ex-date to capture the dividend can win. **Early exercise trades your time value for the dividend**, so it only pays when the dividend is bigger than what you surrender.
cards.depth: This is why deep-in-the-money calls on high-yield names get assigned early, and why short-call holders face assignment risk right before ex-date.
